screens.prompt: In B8, return the name of the rep with the highest score from A2:B7, ranking the table with SORT before you pick a cell.

hints.syntax: =INDEX(SORT(A2:B7,2,-1),1,1): the inner call ranks, the outer call picks.
hints.func-sort: Sort by the score column, highest first. Sorting by name or ascending puts somebody else on top.
hints.func-index: SORT returns a six-row block. INDEX needs a row and a column number to narrow it to one cell.
hints.require-ref: Start the array at A2, not A3. A range from row 3 leaves Ada and her 88 out of the ranking.
hints.value: That is not the top of the ranking. Descending order puts 95 first, so row 1 holds Mia.
hints.error: #VALUE! means the sort index points outside the two columns. An INDEX row beyond row 6 returns #REF!.

reject.why: ranks the table correctly but returns the whole block, so the answer cell holds a spilled range instead of one name
sorts ascending, so the first row is the lowest score
sorts by the rep name instead of the score
picks the second row of the ranking, not the first
hard-codes the row Mia happens to sit on today
returns the score 95 rather than the name attached to it
the sort index is outside the two-column table, so SORT reports #VALUE!
starts below the table and never looks at the scores column from row 2

docs.explain:
SORT returns a new block of rows in the order you ask for, and the source table keeps its own order. The second argument names the column inside that array, so 2 is the score column. The third takes 1 for ascending and -1 for descending.

The six reps hold scores of 88, 95, 72, 91, 61 and 80. Sorting on column 2 descending puts Mia's 95 on the first row and Sam's 61 last. On its own, SORT spills six rows starting at B8, so =INDEX(SORT(A2:B7,2,-1),1,1) asks the ranked block for row 1, column 1: the name at the top.

Change the 1 to 2 and the same formula reads the runner-up, Ivy on 91. The sort index counts columns inside the array, not columns on the sheet, so 3 on this two-column table returns #VALUE!.

errors.text: The sort index is outside the array, or INDEX was given a row without a column.
INDEX asked for a row past the sixth, which the sorted block does not have.
The file is open in an Excel without dynamic arrays, so SORT is not recognised.

docs.atWork: Top customer by revenue, and the latest invoice date, both read from a ranked copy of a small table.
docs.outcome: Rank a table without touching it, then read one cell out of the ranked block.

seo.title: SORT in Excel, then INDEX one cell out
seo.description: SORT ranks a block in the order you ask for without touching the source. INDEX then pulls one cell, so row 1 is the top and row 2 the runner-up.
